rows.task: Our speech-to-text pipeline has a 14.2% word error rate on our 1,200-utterance call-center test set (last nightly run). Lower it.
rows.reply:
I can't see the pipeline or its test set from here, so I haven't reproduced the 14.2% yet. Here is the plan.

**What to beat.** I couldn't find a trustworthy, current state-of-the-art word error rate for call-center audio.
- The nearest outside numbers are old. In 2020, three commercial systems scored 16.5–19.2% on 50 real customer-service calls, and 10.2–11.6% on Switchboard ([Kili 2026 guide](https://kili-technology.com/blog/asr-models-guide-word-error-rate-benchmarks-and-failure-modes-2026)).
- Humans score about 5.9% on Switchboard and 11.3% on the more casual CallHome ([arXiv 1703.02136](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1703.02136)).
- Two careful transcribers disagree with each other 4.1–4.5% of the time on phone speech. That is roughly the floor for any score.
- Vendor "#1" claims, such as [Gladia's](https://www.gladia.io/blog/call-transcription-accuracy-benchmarks-what-contact-centers-should-measure), don't give a number I can check.

So 14.2% is already better than the 2020 call-center results. The real yardstick is current models run on our own audio. My working target is **≤10%** on the same 1,200 utterances, with no category getting worse. I'll revise it once step 4 shows what current models score.

**First steps (on a branch `fix/call-center-wer`)**
1. Read the `.agent/` state (current, progress, experiments, hypotheses) and the climb ledger. I'll pick up any work in progress and skip anything already rejected.
2. Re-run the nightly scoring myself on the real pipeline to confirm 14.2%. I'll record the commit, the model and the text normalizer it used.
3. Break the error down by type (substitutions, deletions, insertions) and by slice: audio quality, speaker (agent or caller), accent, numbers and names, crosstalk, and utterance length. I'll also hand-check about 50 utterances with the worst scores to see how many "errors" are really wrong reference transcripts or normalization mismatches ("$20" vs "twenty dollars"). If they are, cleaning the references fixes the measurement but it isn't a model gain, and I'll report it separately.
4. Run two or three current models on the same 1,200 utterances under the same scoring. This gives the outside comparison I couldn't find published.

**What I'll measure.** Word error rate across the whole set, with a confidence interval from resampling utterances. I'll compare each candidate to the baseline on the same utterances, plus error rates per slice and on names and numbers, and speed and cost. I'll fix the thresholds and set aside a held-out portion before tuning, so I'm not tuning to the test set.

**What I'll build, depending on what step 3 shows**
- Phone-line audio problems: audio conditioning, or a model tuned for phone audio.
- Product names, account numbers and other domain words: biasing the recognizer toward a list of expected terms, plus rules that put numbers into a standard format.
- A weak base model: swap or fine-tune it on call-center audio we transcribe ourselves. This is the bigger architectural option, and I'll take it if the gap calls for it.
- Crosstalk: split the audio by speaker or channel before recognition.

Each candidate gets a hypothesis note saying what result would prove it wrong. I'll keep only what beats the baseline beyond the noise. Scripts go under `scripts/`, outputs under `build/`, and results get logged to `.agent/experiments.jsonl`.

One question: who owns the reference transcripts? If many are wrong, fixing them needs your sign-off.

Sources: [Kili ASR guide 2026](https://kili-technology.com/blog/asr-models-guide-word-error-rate-benchmarks-and-failure-modes-2026), [arXiv 1703.02136](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1703.02136), [Gladia contact-center benchmarks](https://www.gladia.io/blog/call-transcription-accuracy-benchmarks-what-contact-centers-should-measure), [Gladia 8 kHz telephony](https://www.gladia.io/blog/telephony-audio-robustness-why-8khz-narrowband-calls-break-generic-stt), [arXiv 2604.07354](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.07354)

3. **Check that the metric matches the goal.** Overall WER treats "um" the same as a wrong account number. The rules, written down before measuring:

2. Remove wasted or harmful steps: double resampling, voice detection that clips the start of words, chunk boundaries that cut words.
3. Bias the model toward a list of your product names and terms.
4. Beam size and language-model weight, tuned on the development set only.
5. Fine-tuning or a model switch. If it comes to that, I'll compare at equal cost.

- the pipeline repo and the nightly command;
- whether latency and cost limits other than mine apply;
- whether names and numbers matter more than raw WER.

rows.task: Our speech-to-text pipeline has a 14.2% word error rate on our 1,200-utterance call-center test set (last nightly run). Lower it.
rows.reply:
I'll treat 14.2% as the starting point. The number to beat is whatever the best current models score on our own calls.

**The bar (from search; still to verify)**
- **Nearest public result for real call-centre audio:** a 2026 analysis found three commercial systems at 16.5–19.2% WER on contact-centre calls and 10.2–11.6% on Switchboard. It says those checkpoints are out of date ([Kili](https://kili-technology.com/blog/asr-models-guide-word-error-rate-benchmarks-and-failure-modes-2026)). So we may already beat that published range, and I don't trust it as a bar.
- **Best general English result:** Granite Speech 4.1 2B at about 5.3% average and Cohere Transcribe at about 5.4% on the Open ASR Leaderboard. That board has no telephone or Switchboard track ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.06961v2), [mirror](https://benchmarklist.com/benchmarks/open_asr_leaderboard/)).
- **Our limit, not our bar:** trained human transcribers disagree with each other by 4.1–4.5% on telephone speech. If our reference transcripts are noisy, some of the 14.2% is errors in the references, not the model.
- **Working target:** ≤10.0% WER on the 1,200-utterance set, with no subset more than 0.5 points worse. If the best current models score better than that on our audio, their number becomes the target.

**First steps**
1. Read `.agent/current.json`, `progress.md`, `experiments.jsonl`, `hypotheses/` and the climb ledger. I'll pick up any active work and keep the list of rejected approaches.
2. Re-run the nightly pipeline as it actually runs to confirm 14.2%. Then fix the scoring before tuning anything:
   - text normalisation (numbers, contractions, filler words like "uh"/"um", disfluencies);
   - bootstrap confidence intervals over utterances, with calls kept together, so 1,200 utterances don't make a 0.5-point change look real.
3. Break the errors down (`/diagnose`): substitutions vs. deletions vs. insertions, then by audio quality (8 kHz or compression), crosstalk and agent-vs-customer channel, accent, and domain terms (product names, account and number strings). I'll also hand-audit about 100 reference transcripts to estimate how much of the error is in the references.

**Candidates, ranked only after step 3**
- **Swap the model:** run Granite Speech 4.1, Cohere Transcribe, Parakeet/Canary and a commercial API on the same set with the same normalisation. This could be a large drop at low cost.
- **Domain vocabulary:** keyword boosting or contextual biasing, or a domain language model or LLM rescoring pass. Worth doing if domain terms dominate the substitutions.
- **Front end:** split stereo channels, check sample-rate handling, and fix voice-activity-detection segmentation. Worth doing if deletions dominate or there is a lot of crosstalk.
- **Fine-tuning** on our own call audio (8 kHz augmentation, LoRA). This is the bigger change, and only on a strictly separate training split.

Before ranking, I'll run the climb's three passes: why the leading candidate fails two weeks from now, what would make the result ten times better, and the important question nobody has asked. My answer to the last one so far: does WER on entities like names and numbers matter more to the business than overall WER?

**The test and the decision rule**
- One hypothesis file per candidate in `.agent/hypotheses/`.
- Each candidate gets a fixed budget for latency, cost per audio hour and GPU.
- I'll set aside a dev subset for tuning and never look at the decision set while tuning.
- Keep a candidate only if WER is at least 1.0 point lower, the confidence interval excludes zero, and latency or cost stays within budget.

After each decision I'll log the experiment, update the ledger and scorecard, and run `skill-run-log`. If WER is flat for three measurements, I'll switch to a different approach rather than tune harder.

rows.task: Two months of prompt and few-shot changes have kept our invoice field extractor between 87% and 89% of fields correct on 500 labeled invoices. Decide what to try next.
rows.reply:
My recommendation: stop changing the prompt and find out what the remaining 11% of misses actually are. Two months in a 2-point band is a plateau, and part of that band may just be noise, so another few-shot round would be guessing. I read the team's evaluation guides (`claude/skills/eval-engineering/SKILL.md` and `claude/skills/diagnose/references/eval-results.md`). Both say the same thing: check the measurement and a simple baseline before changing the system.

**First steps**
1. **Measure the noise.** Re-run the current best prompt 3–5 times on the same 500 invoices. Then compute a bootstrap interval that resamples whole invoices, because errors cluster by invoice. If the interval is about ±1 point, most of the 87–89% movement was never real, and the prompt history can't tell good changes from bad ones.
2. **Sort every wrong field into one cause**, using the best run (about 550 fields if invoices average 10):
   - The label is wrong.
   - The scorer is wrong: a correct value with a different date, currency or whitespace format.
   - The input is wrong: the value is missing or garbled in the OCR or text layer.
   - The model picked the wrong one of two real candidates, such as ship-to vs bill-to, or subtotal vs total.
   - Line-item or table structure was lost.
   - The model made the value up.
   This tally decides what to try next.
3. **Set the bar.** Have a second person label 50 invoices to get a human agreement rate. Run one prebuilt invoice extractor (for example Azure Document Intelligence's invoice model or AWS Textract AnalyzeExpense) on all 500 through the same scorer. If a prebuilt tool reaches 88% unchanged, the prompt work hasn't added value. If humans agree only 93% of the time, the real gap is smaller than it looks.

**What I'll build, depending on the tally**
- **Labels or scorer:** fix the labels and add normalization before comparison. That alone may raise the score. It is a measurement fix, not a model gain, and I'll report it that way.
- **Input:** improve what the model sees. That means a better OCR or layout step, or sending the page image alongside the text. Prompts can't recover text that isn't there.
- **Picking the wrong candidate:** ask for structured output with a short evidence quote for each field. Add code checks that the line items add up to the subtotal, the subtotal plus tax equals the total, the dates are valid and the dates are in order. When a check fails, retry that field or flag it for review.
- **Concentrated in a few vendors or layouts:** handle those layouts separately or fine-tune on them, and measure on layouts the model hasn't seen.

**How I'll measure**
I'll report accuracy per field and per cause, as well as overall. Each change is compared, invoice by invoice, against the current best prompt and the prebuilt tool. A change only counts if it beats the noise interval from step 1. I'll develop on about 350 invoices and keep 150 aside, used only once for the final decision. Earlier prompt rounds were tuned on all 500, which may have overfit them to this set.

I'll write the results up as a dated note wherever your team keeps working notes, linking the run outputs rather than copying them. If the tally shows most misses are label or input problems, I'll recommend no model change at all.

judgment.q2_quote: A change only counts if it beats the noise interval from step 1.

rows.task: Two months of prompt and few-shot changes have kept our invoice field extractor between 87% and 89% of fields correct on 500 labeled invoices. Decide what to try next.
rows.reply:
I'd stop changing the prompt and find out what the remaining 11–13% of errors actually are before choosing the next fix. Two months inside a 2-point band suggests the prompt changes have been measuring noise, or that something the prompt can't reach is causing most of the failures.

**Why the band probably tells us nothing yet**
- Fields within one invoice tend to succeed or fail together, so the real sample size is closer to 500 invoices than to the number of fields. That puts the noise at roughly ±1.5 points or more, so 87% and 89% may be the same result.
- All the tuning was done on those same 500 invoices. Any gain is likely to be fitted to them and may not carry over to new invoices.

   - The model genuinely got it wrong (wrong field picked, wrong line item, arithmetic).

   Break the results down by field and by vendor or layout. My bet is that one or two causes account for most of the gap.
3. **Find the ceiling.** Have a second person label about 50 invoices. If people only agree on about 93% of fields, 89% is near the ceiling and we should change the target, not the model.

- Human agreement from step 3 as the ceiling.

Some "improvements" and "regressions" were probably indistinguishable. A 2-point band is also what you'd expect if most errors come from something prompts can't change: text missing from the input, wrong labels, or ambiguous normalization.

**First concrete steps**
1. **Fix the baseline.** Run the current prompt 3 times on all 500 invoices. Measure run-to-run spread and a confidence interval that accounts for errors grouping by invoice. That interval is the number to beat. Smaller differences don't count.
2. **Sort the errors by cause.** Take every wrong field and record the field type, the invoice layout or vendor, and the cause:
   - (a) the value is missing or garbled in the OCR or text the model receives;
   - (b) the label is wrong;
   - (c) the answer is right but formatted differently (dates, currency, "Inc." vs no suffix);
   - (d) layout trouble, such as tables, multi-page invoices or line items;
   - (e) the model's reasoning is wrong even though the text is present.
   I'll hand-check about 150 errors and look for any cause, field or vendor that dominates.
3. **Check whether prompts can reach these errors.** Re-run the wrong fields with an oracle fix for each cause: corrected text for (a), a fixed label for (b), a normalized comparison for (c). Each fix shows the most that cause could cost you.

- **Wrong labels or formatting dominate:** fix the labels and the scorer. That's measurement, not model work. I'd report old and new scores side by side so they stay comparable.
- **Missing input text dominates:** a better OCR or layout step, or sending the page image to a vision model. Prompt changes can't recover text that never arrived.
- **Layout dominates:** pull tables and key-value pairs out structurally first, or use templates for the top vendors.
- **Reasoning dominates:** validate the output (totals = subtotal + tax, date sanity checks, vendor-name lookup), retry when a check fails, and route low-confidence fields to a human. This may be cheaper than chasing accuracy.
- **No change:** if what's left is mostly genuinely ambiguous invoices, 88% may be near the ceiling for this data. That's a valid answer.

**Deciding test for the chosen fix.** Run it on the same 500 invoices for at least 3 runs. It's accepted only if it beats the step-1 interval, and no field that matters downstream (total, tax, invoice number) gets worse by more than its own noise. I'll set the cost and latency limits before building, and stop after one complete attempt if it can't clear the interval.

**Pre-mortem.** The most likely way this fails two weeks from now: we tune on the 500 labeled invoices and overfit to them. I'd hold out about 100 invoices, or new production invoices, for the final check.

**The question nobody asked.** Is "percent of fields correct" even the right measure? What the business probably cares about is the share of invoices that go through with no human correction, or the error rate on money fields. A model at 88% of fields could be anywhere from 40% to 80% of invoices fully correct. Step 2 will report both.

rows.task: Our coding agent resolves 22 of 75 tasks in our internal bug-fix benchmark with one model in a single loop. We think the loop design is the limit. Find a better agent design.
rows.reply:
My plan is to first test whether the loop design is really what caps us at 22/75, then compare a few alternative designs against the current loop at the same cost. Only a design that beats it on tasks it never saw gets promoted.

**First steps**
1. **Sort the 53 failures by cause.** I'll read the traces and give each failed task one label for where it went wrong:
   - couldn't find the right code;
   - misunderstood the bug;
   - wrote a wrong patch and didn't notice;
   - patch was right but broke other tests;
   - ran out of turns or context;
   - setup or harness error;
   - unclear task or flawed test.

   Environment and test failures come out of the denominator first. The point is to see whether failures cluster where the loop's shape matters (no step that reproduces the bug, no check before stopping, context filling up) or where the model just can't do the work.
2. **Measure run-to-run variation and pass@k on the current loop.** I'll run all 75 tasks 5 times. If 22 moves by ±4 between runs, a "better design" claim needs repeated runs. If pass@5 is far above 22 (say 35+), the model can already solve those tasks and the problem is picking and checking answers, which points to a selection design. If pass@5 stays near 22, a new loop probably won't help much and the model is the more likely limit. I'll report that rather than build something complicated.
3. **Write the comparison rules down before running anything.** The unit is the task, and every design runs on the same tasks so results can be paired. Each design gets the same token and dollar budget as the baseline; otherwise extra compute could pass for better design. The smallest gain worth having is about +6 tasks. I'll hold back 25 tasks, tune on 50, and promote only if the gain holds on the held-back 25.

**What I'll measure**
- Main metric: tasks resolved under the benchmark's own tests, compared per task against the current single loop at equal cost.
- Also: cost per task, wall time, and regressions (tasks the baseline solves that the new design loses).

**What I'll build** (each candidate is a small change to the existing loop, and the failure sorting decides which go first)
- **Reproduce first:** the agent must write a failing test before it edits code, and can't finish until that test passes and the existing tests still pass.
- **Sample several patches and pick one:** generate k patches within the same budget and choose using test results, with an LLM judge to break ties. Published work shows gains from this kind of selection ([SWE-Gym](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.21139), [LLM-as-a-Verifier](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.05391)).
- **Separate planning and review steps:** a planner, an editor, and a reviewer, each starting from a fresh context. One paper reports a large gain over its own single agent, but it is the authors' evaluation of their own system ([AgentForge](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.13120)). Another finds the model matters more than the scaffold ([DeepSWE](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.07946)), so I'm not assuming this wins.
- **Context management** (summarising or trimming history), only if the failure sorting shows long runs fail more often.

Each result will be one of: promote, reject, keep testing, or inconclusive. I'll use the repo's statistics procedure (`claude/skills/evolve/references/STATS.md`). I'll record the plan, run IDs and raw results in a dated note next to the existing one in `claude/proposals/`. New scripts go under `scripts/`, and run outputs go under `build/`.

- **Why it isn't directly comparable:** That number only reorders a small, already-judged candidate list, and it gives partial credit (0.1 and 0.01) to substitutes and complements. If our 0.41 is measured over the whole catalog, retrieval misses count against us and the 0.9043 overstates what's reachable.
- **Fairer reference:** On Wayfair's WANDS dataset, a small cross-encoder added only +0.039 NDCG@10 over basic rank fusion, and nothing over tuned fusion. Reranking alone may not move us much.
- **Target:** at least 0.50 NDCG@10 on queries we hold back, with no drop in latency or zero-result rate. I'll revise it once I've scored our pipeline on ESCI the way the competition does, so we know how far we really are from the leader.

**First steps**
1. Read the progress and experiment notes in `.agent/` (`current.json`, `progress.md`, `experiments.jsonl`, `hypotheses/`, `pursuits/`) and the climb ledger. Anything already tried and rejected stays rejected.
2. Check the metric before optimizing it:
   - What gain each relevance grade gets and how missing judgments count.
   - Whether the 2,000 queries reflect real traffic.
   - Whether NDCG tracks clicks or conversions.
   - If unjudged results count as irrelevant, the score penalizes new retrieval methods for surfacing products nobody has judged yet.
3. Split the queries now into a set I can tune on and a held-out set that decides. Fix the decision rule before seeing results: a paired bootstrap confidence interval on the difference must exclude zero.
4. Rerun the production pipeline end to end on both sets to get a baseline I measured myself.

**Finding what actually limits the score**
- **Ranking or retrieval?** Measure the best NDCG@10 possible if top-k recall@100/1000 were reordered perfectly. If recall is the gap, a better reranker can't fix it.
- **Where queries fail:** Break failures down by query type (head vs. tail, attribute queries, typos, zero results). Then read about 50 failing queries by hand.

**Options to test, all on the same candidate depth and latency budget**
- **A. Tune what we have:** better field weights, synonyms and spelling correction. This is also the cheap baseline the others must beat.
- **B. If recall limits:** add embedding search alongside keyword search and merge the two with tuned fusion.
- **C. If ordering limits:** a cross-encoder fine-tuned the ESCI way (four classes, weighted score), trained on our judgments plus ESCI. An off-the-shelf model like Qwen3-Reranker comes first as a quick check.
- **D. More training data:** have an LLM label query–product pairs. Its labels have to agree with the existing human judgments before I trust them.

Each option gets a written hypothesis in `.agent/hypotheses/` naming the number to beat and the result that would rule it out. If the metric stays flat for three measurements, I switch approach instead of tuning harder. I'll log every attempt, including failures.

Sources:
- [Shopping Queries Dataset (ESCI)](https://ar5iv.arxiv.org/html/2206.06588)
- [KDD Cup 2022 Task 1 winner](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.02958v1.pdf)
- [Qdrant: When is a reranker worth it](https://qdrant.tech/articles/when-a-reranker-is-worth-it/)
- [WANDS](https://cs.paperswithcode.com/paper/wands-dataset-for-product-search-relevance)

rows.task: Our product search scores NDCG@10 of 0.41 on 2,000 judged queries from last quarter. Improve it.
rows.reply:
I'll aim to take NDCG@10 from 0.41 to at least 0.47 on a held-out half of the 2,000 queries, without going over the current latency budget. I'll only call it done if a paired bootstrap shows the 95% interval of the gain stays above +0.03.

**Why that target.** No public leaderboard covers this directly. The closest outside results I found:
- **Amazon ESCI (US test split):** one unofficial Hugging Face model card reports NDCG@10 going from 0.435 with the retriever alone to 0.516 with a cross-encoder reranker fine-tuned on ESCI. That's about +19% relative. It also reports that an off-the-shelf MS MARCO reranker made ranking worse. I still need to confirm these numbers against papers that cite the dataset.
- **Wayfair WANDS:** Doug Turnbull's careful run found hybrid search beat BM25 by only 1–3% (0.698 → 0.719). Larger gains on the same data (up to 0.75) come from heavy tuning or sources I couldn't trace.

Our 0.41 can't be compared with those numbers directly, because gain scales and candidate pools differ. So I'm using the relative gain as the bar, and 0.47 is about +15%.

**First steps**
1. Read the product repo's `.agent/` state and the climb ledger, so I don't repeat rejected approaches.
2. Check the metric before optimizing it:
   - the relevance scale and gain mapping;
   - how unjudged results in the top 10 are scored (if they count as zero, any new retriever looks worse);
   - whether last quarter's queries still match the current catalog.
3. Fix the dev/held-out split now and record it. I'll tune only on the dev half and leave the thresholds where they are once I see results.
4. Re-run the current eval on the real production path so the 0.41 baseline is reproduced, with confidence intervals.

**Finding what limits the score**
- **Recall:** how many relevant items reach the top 100 and top 1,000 candidates.
- **Ceiling:** the score a perfect reranker would get on the current candidate pool.
- **Where it fails:** errors split by query type (head vs. tail, attribute-heavy, misspelled, zero-result).

If the ceiling is far above 0.41, ranking is the problem. If it's low, retrieval is.

**Candidates**, each with a predicted gain and a result that would rule it out:
- **A. Fine-tuned reranker:** a cross-encoder trained on ESCI plus our clicks or judgments, applied to the top 50–100. Predicted +0.05 to +0.08. It's ruled out if it gains less than 0.02 on dev, or if p95 latency goes over budget.
- **B. Hybrid retrieval:** BM25 plus dense embeddings, merged with rank fusion. Predicted +0.01 to +0.03 (the WANDS results suggest small gains). It's ruled out if recall@100 doesn't improve.
- **C. Query understanding:** pulling out attributes like brand, size and color, plus spelling correction. Only worth it if the error breakdown points there.
- **D. Filling judgment gaps:** an LLM judge, checked against human labels, for unjudged items in the top 10. This is a measurement fix and isn't counted as a score gain.

Before ranking these, I'll do three passes:
- **Failure check:** assume the reranker failed two weeks from now and ask why; likely answers are unjudged results or latency.
- **10× check:** what would make the result ten times better, perhaps learning from clicks.
- **The question nobody has asked:** does NDCG on last quarter's queries actually track conversion?

**What I'll write and build:** a hypothesis file at `.agent/hypotheses/2026-11-19-product-search-ndcg.md` with the bar, the deciding test, the limits, and the regressions I'll accept. Then the diagnostic harness, then candidates tested one at a time against the same baseline. Each candidate ends as KEEP, ITERATE, ABANDON or REGRESSION, logged in `experiments.jsonl` and the ledger.

rows.task: Our call-summary feature has no evaluation beyond spot checks, and support reports that 1 in 8 summaries of long calls omits a customer commitment. Build the evaluation that gates changes to it.
rows.reply:
I'll build a gate that measures one thing: whether every commitment the customer made on a call shows up in its summary. The starting point is the support figure of 1 in 8 long-call summaries missing a commitment (12.5%), but no one has checked that rate against labelled data yet.

**The bar.** I found no public benchmark for missed commitments or action items. The closest work is MESA on the QMSum Mistake dataset: human annotators agreed strongly on omission errors (Krippendorff's alpha 0.83), and GPT-4 Turbo caught only about 76% of partial omissions ([MESA](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.18444v1), [Refining summaries](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.11919v1)). So a generic model judge isn't good enough on its own. Targets:
- Our judge matches human labels with kappa ≥ 0.8 on data it wasn't tuned on.
- It misses no more than 5% of real omissions.
- It confirms or corrects the 12.5% figure with a stated confidence interval.

**First steps**
1. Find the production entrypoint for summaries: the prompt, the model, how long transcripts are split or cut, and the output format. Truncating or splitting long calls is my first suspect, so I'll record each case's transcript length and position.
2. Pull about 250 recorded long calls in which support reported an omission, plus a random sample of long calls without reports.
3. Have two qualified reviewers list every customer commitment in each transcript, without seeing any summary. Each entry records who committed, what they committed to, any deadline, and the transcript span. A third reviewer settles disagreements, and I keep the disagreements. The tool being judged never writes reference labels. About 40 calls go to judge calibration and the rest are held back for the gating decision.

**What I'll build** (on branch `feat/call-summary-commitment-eval`, scripts under `scripts/`, output under `build/`):
- A runner that calls the production summary entrypoint unchanged.
- A judge that checks, for each labelled commitment, whether the summary contains it. It returns present / absent / wrong / cannot-judge, with evidence spans. Missing or malformed output counts as a failure, never a pass. Transcript text is passed to it clearly marked as data, and the calibration set includes transcripts that try to instruct the judge.
- Code checks for anything code can decide, such as whether the named owner and deadline appear.
- Gate settings in the repo's existing config, each with a default and a one-line comment.

**What I'll measure, and against what**
- Per call: the rate of calls with at least one omission, which is the same unit as the support figure.
- Per commitment: the share of commitments that make it into the summary.
- Both are compared candidate vs. current production on the same held-back calls, using a paired test. Each result reports sample counts, run-to-run variation from repeated judging, and cost and latency.
- The gate fails a change that measurably raises the omission rate.

**Before spending on full runs** I'll run the pre-spend check through the exact scoring path:
- Hand-written correct summaries must pass, and copies with one commitment removed or garbled must fail, with more separation than the judge's run-to-run noise.
- I'll check that no labels or setup data leak into what the summariser or judge sees.
- I'll run simple baselines under the same conditions: one that just pulls out every "I'll…/we will…" sentence, and one unguided model attempt. If a baseline ties production, that's a finding to report; I won't make the cases harder so production wins.
- I'll capture one real end-to-end attempt with its trace, usage and cost.

**Blind spots I'll report:** short calls, commitments made by the agent rather than the customer, and implied commitments the reviewers disagree on.

rows.reply:
I'll build a gate that measures one thing directly: how often a summary of a long call leaves out a commitment the customer made. A change merges only if it lowers that rate, or at least doesn't raise it, without inventing commitments. The team's eval-engineering skill sets the rules for this, and the conventions skill sets the file layout. The product code isn't in this checkout, so I haven't run anything yet.

**What we know now.** "1 in 8" comes from calls that support saw and reported, so it's a skewed sample and not our measured rate. It's the figure the first labeled set will check, not the number to beat. I couldn't find a published benchmark for this specific failure, so we'll build the labeled set ourselves.

**First steps**
1. Read the production summary code end to end: the prompt, how long transcripts are cut or split into chunks, the model, and any length limits. Long calls failing more often suggests truncation or a middle section getting dropped, and the cases should catch that.
2. Pull the calls support reported plus a random sample of long calls, about 300 in total, stratified by length. "Long" is the threshold support uses. Add about 100 short calls to catch regressions there.
3. Have two qualified people list each customer commitment per transcript, without seeing any summary. We keep their disagreements and settle them openly. Some calls should have no commitments, and some should have commitments only in the last third of the call.

**What gets measured**
- **Main metric: omission rate.** The share of long calls whose summary misses at least one labeled commitment, plus the share of all commitments missed. Results are reported with sample counts and confidence intervals, comparing a candidate against current production on the same calls.
- **Invented commitments.** Summaries that claim a commitment the customer never made, so a model can't pass by listing everything.
- **Short-call regression, summary length, cost and latency.**
- **Matching.** Code decides what it can, such as a missing summary or a broken format. Whether a summary line captures a labeled commitment is a model judgment. We'll test that judge on a separate set of labeled cases: correct matches, fluent paraphrases that drop the deadline or amount, commitments credited to the wrong person, and transcript text that tries to instruct the judge. We'll record how often it wrongly passes and wrongly fails, and it can return "cannot judge," which never counts as a pass. Missing data fails a case rather than passing it.

**Checks before trusting the gate**
- A good summary and a realistic bad one must score clearly apart.
- Simple baselines run under the same conditions: current production, summarizing only the first N thousand tokens, and a keyword pass for phrases like "we'll" or "I will send." If the keyword pass matches production, that tells us about the cases or the feature, and I'll report it rather than make the cases harder.
- One real run captured in full: outputs, traces, usage.

**What I'll build**
- Branch `feat/call-summary-eval`.
- The case set and labels, in the project's existing runner and record format.
- The judge, with its calibration record.
- `scripts/run-summary-eval.*`, with a first-line comment saying what it does.
- A gate that blocks a change if long-call omission gets worse beyond noise, or invented commitments go up. The threshold is set before we see any candidate results.
- Results written under `build/`.
- The cases that decide the gate are kept separate from the ones used while developing changes.

**The report will include** the commands, where the labels came from, the judge's error rates, the baseline scores, and any gaps, such as commitments split across speakers or calls in other languages.

2. **Pull the support tickets** behind the 1-in-8 figure. - **Code checks**: the output matches its schema, and it stays within the length limit. A summary that just copies the transcript has to fail.
- **A model judge that checks each commitment.** For each labeled commitment it answers present, missing, or distorted (wrong owner, date, or certainty), or "cannot judge", and quotes the summary text it relied on. It also flags commitments in the summary that aren't in the transcript. Its output is validated, and missing or malformed output counts as a fail. Every call is logged with model, prompt, input hash, and raw and parsed output.
- **The gate**: commitment recall on long calls, plus the rate of invented commitments. A change can't ship if it lowers recall or adds invented commitments beyond what run-to-run noise explains. Errors in the harness or judge are counted separately and never treated as a pass. With 200 long calls, a 12.5% miss rate has about ±2.3 points of noise, so the suite can catch a regression of roughly 5 points. I'll increase the sample size if the team needs finer detection.

- **Test fixtures**: a hand-written good summary for each of several transcripts, plus copies with one commitment removed, a wrong due date, swapped owner, or a firm promise softened to a maybe. I'll add borderline items like "I'll try to" and a transcript containing an instruction aimed at the judge.

- **Baselines under the same conditions**: today's production summarizer, which should come out near 1 in 8 if the measurement matches what support sees; one plain prompt with no special handling; and a simple keyword pull of "I'll / we will" sentences. If the keyword pull matches production on recall, it shows the gate needs the length and usefulness checks too.
- **One real end-to-end run**, then I'll check that the judge saw the actual summary and labels, and that the recall numbers are nonzero and plausible. After that I'll fill in coverage of short calls and the other failure types, holding some cases back for final comparisons.

I need from you: access to the product repo and transcripts (with personal data scrubbed), and who can do the commitment labeling.

  - keyword matching on "will / I'll / by Friday";

rows.task: Write the analysis of whether our agent's code-execution sandbox should move from containers to microVMs. Container starts take a median 1.9 s, and we had two sandbox-escape findings this year.
rows.reply:
I'll write this as a decision analysis, not a recommendation I've already made. Neither number points to microVMs yet.

**Why I'm not concluding yet**
- **The 1.9 s start time is probably not the cost of using containers.** A container usually starts in a few hundred milliseconds on a warm host. A median of 1.9 s suggests time going to image pulls, filesystem setup, network setup or dependency install. MicroVMs pay most of those same costs. Firecracker-class VMs start fast only when restored from a snapshot or taken from a warm pool, and a container can use the same tricks. So switching could leave the latency about where it is.
- **Two escapes don't show that the shared kernel is the problem.** A microVM fixes escapes that go through the shared host kernel. It doesn't fix a mounted Docker socket, privileged mode, a credential in the environment, open network egress or a host path mount. Those would escape a VM too.

**First steps**
1. Pull the two findings and sort each one as either a kernel/runtime escape or a configuration/privilege escape. That decides the security half of the case.
2. Break the 1.9 s down by phase from traces or by timing a start step by step: scheduling, image pull, rootfs, network, runtime init, agent ready. I'll report the median, p95 and p99 for each phase, not just the overall median.
3. Find out what share of starts are cold (image not cached).

**What I'll measure, and against what**
I'll run the same workload and image on four setups:
- the current containers
- the current containers with a warm pool and pre-pulled images (the cheapest fix)
- gVisor (a kernel boundary without VMs)
- Firecracker or Kata, both cold boot and snapshot restore

For each I'll record:
- time to the first command running (median, p95, p99) over at least 200 starts
- memory overhead per sandbox and sandboxes per host
- run-time overhead on a typical agent job, both CPU-heavy and file-system-heavy
- whether each of the two findings, replayed, is still exploitable
- operating cost: does it need nested virtualisation or bare-metal hosts, and how much image-pipeline work it adds

**What I'll build**
- A script under `scripts/` (first-line comment saying what it does) that runs the start benchmark on each setup and writes raw results to `build/`.
- Replay cases for the two findings, so the security claim is tested rather than assumed.
- The analysis note itself, dated 2026-11-19 with a title. This repo has no folder for decision notes; the closest are `claude/proposals/<topic>/<date>.md` and `claude/analysis/`. I'll ask which you prefer rather than invent a new one.

**How the note will be organised**
It will cover the decision and the options, then the start-time breakdown, the classification of the two escapes, the comparison table, cost and migration work, and a recommendation with the conditions that would reverse it.

**Where I expect it to land**
- If both escapes went through the kernel: microVMs with snapshot restore, which fix both problems at once.
- If they were configuration issues: fix the configuration and add a warm pool first, then consider gVisor or microVMs as defence in depth.

Since this turn was read-only, nothing is written or measured yet. I need the two findings and start traces to begin.

rows.task: Write the analysis of whether our agent's code-execution sandbox should move from containers to microVMs. Container starts take a median 1.9 s, and we had two sandbox-escape findings this year.
rows.reply:
I'll write this as a decision page that breaks both inputs down by cause. Neither number decides the move by itself. A median start of `1.9 s` doesn't say which phase is slow. And `2` escape findings matter here only if both came from the shared host kernel, since that is the only escape class a microVM removes.

**What I'll correct up front.** The case for microVMs usually rests on Firecracker's `≤125 ms` boot. That figure runs from the start API call to the guest's first process, on a stripped-down kernel and file system ([spec](https://github.com/roypat/firecracker/blob/main/SPECIFICATION.md), a fork I'll check against upstream). It leaves out pulling the image, building the root file system, setting up networking and warming up the runtime. It also isn't a snapshot-restore figure: the restore timings I found are secondary and disagree (~150 ms against microseconds). Restoring one snapshot into many VMs needs [extra protection](https://rywalker.com/research/firecracker). So I'll treat the speed gain as a target, not a fact.

**First steps**
1. **Start-time breakdown.** Pull the raw container start records for the year, not the median. I'll report the median, 95th and 99th percentiles, the count, and the share each phase takes: scheduling, image pull, layer unpack, runtime create, network setup, and in-sandbox init until the first command runs. I'll split cold from warm starts. If most of the `1.9 s` is image pull or init, a microVM won't fix it. A warm pool or pre-pulled images would.
2. **Escape findings.** For each of the two reports I'll record date, vector and root cause. Then I'll sort them into: shared-kernel bug (a microVM fixes it), container runtime or configuration error (also fixable by hardening), and leaks through network egress, mounted secrets or credentials (a microVM doesn't fix those). I'll keep the trigger separate from the cause. With n=2, I'll show the count and won't quote a rate.
3. **Outside comparison.** I'll put containers, gVisor, Kata and Firecracker side by side on start time, density, I/O overhead and escape classes closed. I'll cite only the owners' own docs and specs.
4. **Cost and constraints.** Microvms need hardware virtualization (nested virtualization on our cloud hosts?), so I'll check that, plus memory per sandbox and the GPU and file-mount features the agent uses.

**Measured against what**
- Start time: our current distribution against the target the agent's user experience needs. If nobody has set one, I'll ask rather than invent it.
- Security: escapes closed per option, out of the 2 found.
- Rejection test: if neither escape was kernel-level, the security case falls apart. If image pull and init take more than half the `1.9 s`, the speed case does too.

**What I'll build**
A page at `~/reviews/2026-11-19-sandbox-microvm.html`, made with the brief kit:
- a stacked bar of where the start time goes;
- a table of the escape causes;
- the outside comparison;
- the options with risk and effort for each: harden containers, adopt gVisor, or run a Firecracker pilot;
- one recommended decision, whether it can be reversed, and the cheapest check: a one-week pilot timing Firecracker on our own image against the same phase breakdown.

I'll score the page with `brief-judge`, fix its weakest parts and log the run.

I need from you: where the start records live and the two escape reports.

rows.reply:
I'm going to treat this as a decision memo, not a write-up that assumes the answer. Neither of your two numbers settles the move yet.

**Why neither number decides it yet**
- **The 1.9 s median start may not get faster.** A peer-reviewed Kubernetes benchmark timed full container start at under 0.7 s for Docker and gVisor, 1.9 s for Kata and about 2.4 s for Firecracker ([Edera, arXiv 2501.04580](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.04580)). The fast boot figures people quote come from vendor blogs and restored VM snapshots: around 125 ms ([LWN](https://lwn.net/Articles/775736)) and 28 ms from snapshots ([dev.to](https://dev.to/adwitiya/how-i-built-sandboxes-that-boot-in-28ms-using-firecracker-snapshots-i0k)). So 1.9 s for plain containers suggests the time goes to image pulls or setup, not to the runtime. A microVM won't remove that time unless we also add snapshots.
- **Two findings only justify a microVM if a VM boundary would have stopped them.** A host-kernel or runtime escape would have been stopped. A mounted secret, open network egress or an over-scoped credential would get through a VM unchanged.

**First steps**
1. Pull this year's sandbox start records. Report p50/p95/p99 with the sample size, window and source, and confirm the 1.9 s median against the raw rows. Then split each start into image pull, runtime create, network setup, and workspace and tool setup, and check that the parts add up to the total.
2. Read both escape findings from their original reports. For each, record the root cause separately from the trigger, which boundary it crossed, and whether a microVM, gVisor or a config fix would have blocked it. Mark anything not stated in the report as inferred.
3. Benchmark on our own workload, with the same image, host class and concurrency: the current runtime, gVisor, Firecracker cold boot and Firecracker snapshot restore. For each, measure start-time percentiles, runtime overhead on a representative agent task, memory per sandbox, sandboxes per host, and cost per 1,000 runs. The vendor numbers disagree too much to use, so these runs replace them.

**What I'll judge it against**
- **Latency:** the start target the product needs. If we haven't set one, I'll flag that as the reader's first decision, not invent one.
- **Security:** how many of the 2 findings each option would have blocked, out of 2.
- **Cost:** the change in host count and engineering effort, with a note on whether the move can be undone.

**What I'll build**
- A brief-kit page at `~/reviews/2026-11-19-sandbox-microvm.html`. It leads with the recommendation and its deciding number.
- A start-time chart split by component for each runtime, drawn against the latency target.
- A table showing which option would have blocked each finding.
- A side-by-side table of all four runtimes with every measured field.
- A list of decisions for you, each with a recommendation, its tradeoff and whether it can be reversed.

The likely outcomes are: move, fix the setup steps first, or a narrower switch to gVisor. Each comes with the cheapest check that could prove it wrong. I'll score the page with `brief-judge`, fix its weakest dimensions, and log the run with `skill-run-log`.

**What I need from you:** this session is read-only, and the start records and finding reports aren't in this repository. Send their locations, or approve running the queries and benchmarks.

rows.task: Write the analysis of whether our agent's code-execution sandbox should move from containers to microVMs. Container starts take a median 1.9 s, and we had two sandbox-escape findings this year.
rows.reply:
I'll write this as a decision brief. It will answer one question: does moving to microVMs fix both problems, the 1.9 s starts and the escapes, or only one? It will end with a call: move, harden containers, take a middle step (gVisor), or run the check that settles it first.

**The bar I'll measure against (checked today):**
- **Firecracker's own spec:** at most 125 ms from the start call to the guest's first process. That uses a minimal kernel and no serial console, and it stops before any user code runs ([spec](https://github.com/roypat/firecracker/blob/main/SPECIFICATION.md)).
- **Independent benchmark:** E2B (Firecracker) took 717 ms to create a sandbox and 662 ms to resume one. Modal (gVisor) took 2347 ms to boot from a snapshot ([LogRocket](https://blog.logrocket.com/comparing-ai-agent-sandbox-platforms-e2b-modal-daytona-and-more/)). Vendors claim about 150 ms or less, but no one has verified those numbers, so I'll label them as claims.
- **Our number:** 1.9 s median. Even the independent result is about 2.7× faster, so a target near 700 ms at p50 is plausible. That target only holds if the time goes where a VM would save it.

**First steps:**
1. **Break down the 1.9 s.** I'll pull the start-latency records with their count, time window, p50, p95 and p99, and split each start into stages: image pull or unpack, runtime create, network setup, filesystem mount, and the language runtime getting ready. If most of the time is image pull or interpreter warm-up, a microVM won't fix it, and a warm pool or snapshots would. Containers can use those too. The chart will show the stages as parts of the whole start time.
2. **Classify the two escape findings.** For each one I'll record which layer failed: shared host kernel, container runtime, a misconfiguration (privileged mode, mounted Docker socket, missing seccomp filter), or network/credential exposure. Only a shared-kernel or runtime break is something a microVM structurally prevents. A config or network failure would happen again inside a VM. I'll cite each finding's own write-up, not summaries of it.
3. **Prior art and costs.** I'll check how Firecracker, Kata, Cloud Hypervisor and gVisor compare on isolation, syscall overhead (one guide puts gVisor at 10–20%), memory density, whether they need nested virtualization on our hosts, and snapshot caveats. Restoring one snapshot into many VMs is documented as insecure unless you mitigate it.
4. **A test that could prove me wrong.** I'll propose one Firecracker prototype running our real image and first tool call. The claim fails if p50 is not under about 700 ms with n of at least 200, or if either escape class reproduces inside it.

**What I'll build:** a page at `~/reviews/2026-11-19-sandbox-microvm.html`, made with the brief kit:
- a scoreboard of our numbers against the bar
- a chart of where the start time goes
- a table of each finding against which layer would have stopped it
- an options table with latency, isolation, cost and migration effort, keeping every measured column
- a pre-mortem on the recommendation

I'll separate what I observed from what I project. I'll score the page with `brief-judge`, fix its weakest parts, and log the run.

**What I expect:** if at least one escape is a kernel or runtime break and the start time is mostly runtime overhead, the answer is to move. If both escapes are config failures and the start time is image pull, the answer is to harden the containers and add a warm pool. That's much cheaper and fixes both problems.

Sources: [Firecracker spec](https://github.com/roypat/firecracker/blob/main/SPECIFICATION.md), [LogRocket sandbox comparison](https://blog.logrocket.com/comparing-ai-agent-sandbox-platforms-e2b-modal-daytona-and-more/), [Beam 2026](https://www.beam.cloud/blog/best-stateful-sandbox-code-execution-2026), [Firecracker vs Docker](https://huggingface.co/blog/agentbox-master/firecracker-vs-docker-tech-boundary), [Northflank](https://northflank.com/blog/firecracker-vs-cloud-hypervisor)

**The bar so far (public sources):**

Our 1.9 s median start is roughly 3–15× those numbers.

I'll show this as a chart of where the time goes, with the median, the 99th percentile and the sample size. If most of it is image pull or network setup, a microVM keeps that cost, and a warm pool or pre-pulled images would get most of the gain without a migration.
2. **Sort the two escape findings by cause.** For each one, I'll record whether it came from the shared host kernel (which a microVM removes) or from something else: a mounted volume, an exposed socket, open network access to cloud metadata, leaked credentials, or extra container privileges. A microVM fixes only the first kind. If both were the second kind, the case for moving falls apart, and the honest answer is to fix the configuration.
3. **Include gVisor.** It's the middle option between containers and microVMs (Modal uses it), and I'll compare it on the same terms.

**What I'll measure:** I'll run 1,000 starts of each option on our own hosts with our sandbox image: containers today, Firecracker cold boot, Firecracker restore from a snapshot, and gVisor. **Proposed target:** starts under 500 ms at the median and under 1 s at the 99th percentile. I'll also check that each escape we had, rewritten as a test, can no longer reach the host. The recommendation must meet both parts, and fixing only one is not enough.

The check that could refute the move: if most of the 1.9 s is not runtime startup, or neither escape involved the kernel, I'll recommend a warm pool plus configuration fixes instead.

The next step after that depends on the result. If the breakdown is surprising, I'll do a root-cause pass. If there's a clear gap, I'll prototype the warm pool or snapshot restore.

rows.task: Build an agent that triages incoming bug reports with component and severity. Today a person triages them, and 23% of bugs are later reassigned to a different component.
rows.reply:
I'll measure before I build anything that writes to the tracker. Your 23% reassignment rate is the bar: it means today's human picks the final component about 77% of the time. But it's a rough measure. Some reassignments happen because the bug turned out to be something else, not because triage got it wrong. I don't have the bug tracker in this read-only repo, so the steps below are a plan.

**Bar**
- **Human:** about 77% top-1 component accuracy, taken from the 23% reassignment rate. I'll recompute it from history, and count reassignments that happened after a root-cause change separately.
- **Published:** the best academic result I found for top-1 component accuracy is 68% on Mozilla and 64% on Eclipse ([DeepTriag, ICPC 2023](https://conf.researchr.org/details/icpc-2023/icpc-2023-research/15/Still-Confusing-for-Bug-Component-Triaging-Deep-Feature-Learning-and-Ensemble-Settin)). Recent fine-tuned LLMs report gains, but mostly on developer assignment ([LIA](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.01780v2), [constrained decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.21156)). None of them measure reassignment directly.
- **Target:** at least 85% top-1 component accuracy on bugs the agent labels itself. Low-confidence bugs go to a person, and that share gets reported too. The aim is to cut reassignments from 23% to 15% or less.
- **Severity:** no number was given, so the human figure comes from history: how often the first severity equals the final one.

**First steps**
1. Export 12+ months of closed bugs with the first and final component, the first and final severity, and timestamps. Split by time: older bugs for development, the newest 1,000+ held out for the final decision.
2. Label 100–200 bugs by hand to sort reassignments into "triage error" and "scope changed". That tells me how much of the 23% any triager could actually fix.
3. Run simple baselines through the same scoring path: always the most common component, a keyword/TF-IDF classifier, and a single unguided LLM prompt. If the agent can't clearly beat the TF-IDF classifier, I'll say so and not make the cases harder to force a win.

**What I'll measure**
For components: top-1 and top-3 accuracy against the final component, and the reassignment rate the agent's labels would have produced. For severity: exact match and how often it's off by more than one level. Also accuracy at each confidence level, which sets where low-confidence bugs go to a person. Plus cost and time per bug, with variation over repeated runs. Labels the agent was built against stay separate from the held-out set.

**What I'll build**
- An agent that reads the report, the component list and owners, and similar past bugs. It returns a component, a severity, a confidence score and a short reason through a validated tool.
- At first it runs in suggest-only mode, posting a comment or a draft label. It changes fields in the tracker only when you allow it per component, and only above the confidence threshold. Retries won't post duplicates.
- A shadow run next to the human triager for 2–4 weeks, comparing both against the final labels before it labels anything itself.
- An eval harness with `scripts/` entries, each starting with a comment that says what it does. Outputs go under `build/`. Work happens on `feat/bug-triage-agent`, with formatting-only changes in their own commits.

**I need from you:** read access to the tracker export, the current list of components and owners, and the severity definitions.

rows.task: Build an agent that triages incoming bug reports with component and severity. Today a person triages them, and 23% of bugs are later reassigned to a different component.
rows.reply:
I'll treat this as a measurement problem first and an agent second. The 23% is the only number we have, and it's a proxy, not a label.

**Where the bar stands**
- **Best published result:** I ran one search and found nothing that reports LLM component accuracy as a reassignment rate. The closest numbers come from supervised models on public data. DEEPTRIAG gets 68.3% top-1 component accuracy on Mozilla and 64.1% on Eclipse ([ICPC'23](https://conf.researchr.org/details/icpc-2023/icpc-2023-research/15/Still-Confusing-for-Bug-Component-Triaging-Deep-Feature-Learning-and-Ensemble-Settin)). DeBERTa gets F1 0.815 on Eclipse JDT and 0.637 on Mozilla Core, which has 105 components and where DeBERTa only ties an SVM ([arXiv 2310.06913](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.06913)). LLM papers mostly report developer assignment, not component ([LIA](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.01780v2), [2508.21156](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.21156)).
- **Our number:** a 23% reassignment rate, so about 77% of first assignments stick. That already beats the published results, so a generic classifier is not the target. Severity has no baseline yet.
- **Target:** fewer than 12% reassigned among the bugs the agent routes on its own, while it handles at least 70% of incoming bugs. Anything it isn't confident about goes to the human. For severity, the target is to match how often two human triagers agree with each other.

**First steps**
1. **Get the data.** I need an export of the tracker history: report text, first and final component, first and final severity, timestamps and reassignment comments. The product isn't in this repo, so this is the blocker.
2. **Clean the label.** The final component is the label, except where the bug was reassigned because new information arrived later. In those cases the first triage wasn't wrong. I'll sample 100 reassignments and classify why each one happened. Until then, 23% is not a clean error rate.
3. **Measure human agreement.** Two triagers independently label 150 bugs for component and severity. That sets the ceiling a model can't meaningfully beat.
4. **Split by time.** Cases for developing the agent come from older months. Final decision cases come from the most recent ones, so nothing leaks from the future.

**Baselines, run under the same conditions as the agent**
- Always pick the most common component.
- Keyword and code-owner lookup: map file paths in stack traces to components.
- TF-IDF with logistic regression.
- One unguided LLM call given only the component list.

If the agent doesn't beat the TF-IDF baseline by more than the run-to-run noise, that tells us something about the data, and I report it as that.

**What I'll build**
- **Inputs:** the component catalog with owners and descriptions, a map from code paths to components, and the 10 most similar resolved bugs from the index.
- **Output:** the LLM returns component, severity, a short rationale and a confidence score.
- **Abstain threshold:** set on the development cases so that precision on the routed bugs meets the target.
- **Shadow mode:** for two to four weeks the agent's labels are logged next to the human's but aren't applied. Live success means its label matches the final component and the bug isn't reassigned.

**What I'll measure**
- Top-1 and top-3 component accuracy.
- Severity agreement, scored so that being off by two levels counts worse than being off by one.
- Reassignment rate at each coverage level, compared with the 23% human rate and the baselines.
- Cost and latency per bug.

All of this goes on a `feat/bug-triage-agent` branch. Evaluation scripts go under `scripts/` and generated outputs under `build/`, as the repo conventions require.

**What I need from you:** access to the tracker export, and someone to define the severity levels.

rows.reply:
I've read the skill and its integrations reference. The product code isn't in this repo, so this plan is based on your brief. The main thing to know up front: the 23% figure is the bar to beat, but it isn't ground truth yet.

**Turning the 23% into a real target**
- Some reassignments fix a wrong first triage. Others happen because the bug turned out to be something else, or because teams reorganized. If I count all of them as misroutes, I'll overstate the human error rate, and the agent will learn from noisy labels.
- Your brief has no severity number. I'll measure how often severity gets changed later (the human's own disagreement rate) before setting any severity target.

**First steps**
1. Find the tracker (Jira, GitHub, Linear, etc.) and its existing component list, severity scale, triage permissions and webhook setup. I'll reuse the existing connector and credentials, kept on the server side.
2. Pull about 6–12 months of closed bugs, recording each one's first component, final component, severity changes and the reason for each change. I'll split them by time, so the held-out set is newer than anything the agent sees.
3. Hand-label a stratified sample of about 200 reassigned bugs as "the first triage was wrong" or "the scope changed." Then build the eval set from final component and final severity, with scope-change cases removed.

**What I'll measure, and against what**
- **Component:** top-1 accuracy on the held-out set, compared with the human's first assignment on the same bugs. That's 77% if all 23% were real misroutes, and probably higher once relabeled. Also top-3 accuracy, and accuracy by component, so rare components don't hide behind the average.
- **Severity:** exact match, plus how often it's wrong by more than one level. Under-calling a critical bug gets its own count because it costs the most.
- **Calibration:** accuracy at each confidence level, so the agent can set "auto-apply" and "ask a human" thresholds.
- **Operational:** time to triage, cost per bug, and how often a human has to step in, all compared with the current person-triage process.

**What I'll build**
- A webhook intake that verifies signatures and deduplicates by issue ID, so a retried delivery doesn't triage twice.
- An agent step whose output is checked against a schema: the component must be in the live component list, severity must be on your scale, and each result carries a confidence score and a short rationale.
- **Shadow mode first:** the agent suggests a triage in a comment or private field, the human still decides, and we log agreement.
- After it beats the baseline, it applies triage on its own only above the confidence threshold. Below the threshold it goes to the human queue, and it never applies critical severity without approval. Every write is idempotent and recorded with the run ID and model version.
- **Feedback loop:** later reassignments are tagged as eval cases. Changes to the prompt or model must re-pass the held-out set and stay easy to roll back.

**Proof before I call it done**
- One real bug runs end to end in a tracker test project: the webhook fires, the suggestion is stored, one approved write happens exactly once, a duplicate delivery is ignored, and a write the agent lacks permission for is denied and logged.
- Then the reassignment rate in shadow mode, compared with the human baseline over the same weeks.

**Questions for you**
- Which tracker do you use?
- Who can approve severity changes?
- Is acting on its own allowed at all, or should it only ever suggest?

When it's done I'll log the run with `skill-run-log /build-agent-app`. Likely next step: `/eval-engineering` for the labeled set.

rows.reply:
I'll start by measuring, before I build anything. The 23% is your only number so far, and it isn't yet an accuracy number I can test against.

**The bar**
1. **Best published result:** I couldn't find a published absolute accuracy for assigning bugs to components with current LLMs. TriagerX reports gains of up to 10% on component suggestions, but only relative to older methods on IBM data. The LLM triage papers I found assign developers, not components. So the real baseline is your person's first assignment.
2. **Our number:** 23% of bugs are reassigned to another component. Severity has no number yet. Some reassignments happen because ownership changed, not because the triager was wrong, so I'll correct for that first.
3. **Target:** 10% or fewer bugs end up in a different component than the agent picked, counting every report including ones it hands back, with each report done in seconds instead of waiting in a queue. Severity should match the final severity at least as often as the person's first call did. I'll fix the exact severity number once the history gives a baseline.
4. **Approach:** Not just a prompt. The agent pulls up similar bugs that were already resolved, along with their final component. It also maps file paths in stack traces and file references to component owners using CODEOWNERS. It can only choose from your valid component list, and it returns a confidence score. When it isn't confident, it hands the bug to the person with its best two guesses.
5. **Outside check:** A held-out set of past bugs from the most recent months, scored against their final component and severity. The person's first assignment on the same bugs is the comparison. It fails if the agent isn't clearly better than the person's first assignment, or if it hands more than about 30% of bugs back to the person.

**First steps**
1. Find out which bug tracker you use (Jira, GitHub or Linear) and confirm which client libraries are installed. Then export about 12 months of reports with their first and final component and severity.
2. Label each reassignment as a misroute or an ownership change, and recompute the baseline.
3. Build the replay test before the agent, so every version is scored on the same set.

**What I'll build**
- **Intake:** a webhook that checks the tracker's signature before trusting anything in the payload. A redelivered event won't apply the result twice.
- **Triage step:** retrieval of similar past bugs and code owners, then a typed tool that returns `{component, severity, confidence, evidence}`, checked against the component list. Free text from the model can never change a ticket.
- **Writing to the tracker:** at first the agent only comments with its suggestion. It sets the fields itself only when the confidence is above a threshold you approve, stored as a policy per project. Tracker credentials stay on the server, and every action is logged, including refusals and failures.
- **Feedback loop:** a person's correction goes back into the pool of past bugs the agent compares against, and the live reassignment rate goes on a dashboard.

**Live proof**
I'll run one real report through a test project in your tracker and confirm:
- the field is set exactly once;
- a redelivered webhook is ignored;
- a write from an account without access is denied;
- a revoked credential shows up as an error, not as "no result";
- the result appears correctly in the tracker.

After launch, the outside check is the live reassignment rate compared with 23%.

**Still missing:** I can't start until you tell me the tracker, give me access to the export, and approve the threshold for automatic updates. Next I'll use `/eval-engineering` to build the replay test.

1. **Split the 2.4% by cause.** Take the undelivered webhooks from the last 30 days and put each into one bucket:
   - Never queued (lost when a service crashed between the event and the first send).
   - Gave up too early (out of attempts, or a short retry window).
   - Wrongly treated as permanent (for example a 429 or 503 handled like a 4xx).
   - Dropped where two of the three services pass a delivery between them.
   - Endpoint really dead (down for days).

   Each bucket needs a different fix. Only the last one can't be fixed on our side.
2. **List the three implementations side by side.** For each one: attempt limit, backoff, jitter, which errors it treats as permanent, where its state lives, and what happens when a process restarts mid-retry. Also find callers that change together, and past incidents traced to differences between the three.
3. **Set the bar.** Compare against Svix and Stripe webhook retries (spaced attempts with jitter over a long window, a final failed state, manual replay, idempotency headers). I'll confirm their exact schedules from their docs before relying on them.

**What I'll measure, and against what**
- **Undelivered rate:** 2.4% today. Target: only the dead-endpoint bucket is left, and each of those webhooks is visible and can be replayed. I'll set the number once the split is done.
- **Implementations:** 3 today, 1 at the end. The check that it worked is all callers moved over and the three old versions deleted.
- **Webhooks lost when a process restarts:** must be 0. I'll prove this with a test that kills the worker partway through retrying.

**What I'll build:** a `delivery-scheduler` module with a small interface:
- `enqueue(delivery)`: written in the same database transaction as the event that triggers it, so the event can't be committed without its delivery.
- `recordAttempt(deliveryId, outcome)` returns the next step: retry at a given time, delivered, or permanently failed.
- `replay(deliveryId)` sends a permanently failed delivery again.

Inside the module:
- **Retry policy:** a pure function, tested on its own, deciding which errors are permanent and when to try next (exponential backoff with full jitter; honours Retry-After).
- **Per-endpoint circuit breaker:** stops hammering an endpoint that keeps failing.
- **Idempotency key on every attempt:** receivers can safely ignore duplicates.
- **Storage:** one Postgres adapter for production and PGlite in tests, with no mocks.

I'll test it through those three calls only. I'll also sketch three or four other interface options and recommend one against the bar.

**Conventions**
- Settle the terms *webhook*, *delivery* and *attempt* in `CONTEXT.md`, using whatever the oldest service already calls them.
- Write an ADR for the decision to use a durable queue written in the same transaction instead of in-memory retries.
- Work on a branch called `feat/webhook-delivery-scheduler`, with one commit per logical step: add the module, move each service over in its own commit, then delete the old code.

Do you have the delivery logs, or should I use the database tables, for the split in step 1?

rows.task: Design the module that schedules retries for our webhook deliveries. Retry logic lives in three services today, and 2.4% of webhooks are never delivered.
rows.reply:
I'll start by measuring what makes up the 2.4%, then build one deep module that replaces the retry logic in all three services. This is a plan only: I could only read here, and the services' code isn't in this checkout.

**What I checked.** The repo has no `CONTEXT.md` and no `docs/adr/`, so I'll propose the terms myself. I also looked up Svix as the best known result: it retries immediately, then after 5s, 5m, 30m, 2h, 5h and 10h. It keeps the same message ID on every retry and sends an "exhausted" event when it gives up. It doesn't promise guaranteed delivery.

**The bar**
1. **Best known result:** Svix's bounded retry window, as above. I found no published figure for its permanent-loss rate.
2. **Our number:** 2.4% of webhooks are never delivered, but we don't yet know the denominator or why each one failed.
3. **Target:** zero deliveries lost silently. A webhook may end undelivered only when its endpoint stayed down for the whole retry window, and the customer must be told when that happens.
4. **Mechanism:** a single durable retry schedule stored in the database, replacing three separate retry loops.
5. **Outside check:** we replay production delivery logs and run tests against a real endpoint that fails, then recovers. It passes when no delivery is lost without a record and every exhausted delivery has an alert.

**First steps**
1. Read all three implementations and map each caller, retry policy and failure path. I'll also count how often a change to one forced changes to the others.
2. Sort the never-delivered webhooks by cause:
   - **Never scheduled:** the retry lived only in memory, or a restart or deploy dropped it.
   - **Wrongly given up:** a 429, 5xx or timeout was treated as permanent.
   - **Truly exhausted:** the endpoint stayed down past the window.
   
   The split decides what matters most. If most fall in the first two groups, durability and correct error classes fix them and the backoff curve barely matters.

**Interface options**
- (a) One call per attempt: `record(deliveryId, outcome)` returns the next attempt time or "exhausted".
- (b) A configurable policy engine, with backoff and classification settings per service.
- (c) A durable outbox: callers run `enqueue(webhook)` once, and the module owns attempts, backoff, idempotency keys and exhaustion events.
- (d) Ports and adapters with a scheduler port.

**I recommend (c).** It has the most depth: callers learn one call plus an event to subscribe to. It also puts the three services' retry code in one place, and it passes the deletion test because removing it would bring the complexity back in three places.

It needs two seams, each with two real adapters:
- **Store:** Postgres in production, PGlite in tests.
- **Transport:** HTTP to real endpoints, and in tests an endpoint we control that is scripted to fail and recover.

The clock is passed in as a dependency. All tests go through `enqueue` and the exhaustion event, with no mocks.

**Terms for `CONTEXT.md`**
- **Delivery:** one webhook to one endpoint. _Avoid_ "message" and "job".
- **Attempt:** one HTTP try at a delivery.
- **Retry window:** the time from the first attempt until the delivery is exhausted.
- **Exhausted:** a delivery whose window ran out, which then produces an exhaustion event to the customer.

**One ADR:** retries are stored durably in our own database rather than in each service's queue. The alternative is a hosted service like Svix, so it's a real choice that is hard to reverse.

**What will show it worked:** all three services migrated to `enqueue`, all three old retry implementations and their tests deleted, and the never-delivered rate (with its denominator stated) below 0.1% of deliveries to endpoints that were reachable. Every exhausted delivery must also carry an alert.

After that comes `/tdd` on the `enqueue` interface, then `/simplify` to remove the old code paths. I'll log the run as `skill-run-log /codebase-design --target "webhook retry scheduling" --verdict PARTIAL --next /tdd`.

Sources:
- [Svix Retry Schedule](https://docs.svix.com/retries)
- [Svix webhook retry strategies](https://www.svix.com/resources/webhook-university/reliability/webhook-retry-strategies/)
- [Hookdeck outbound retry best practices](https://hookdeck.com/outpost/guides/outbound-webhook-retry-best-practices)
